414.title: What you think about often
414.hook: whatever one thinks about often, the mind inclines that way (MN 19)
414.howItsDone: Buddhist practitioners cultivate wholesome thoughts deliberately, for example through loving-kindness practice or recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, on the understanding that repeated thoughts shape the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the honeyball, and your line, the thoughts multiply. Did you catch one thought becoming three, and go back to what you actually saw or heard? Day four hundred fourteen.

Walk the same way across a lawn every day for a month, and you'll make a path. Nobody planned it. Nobody poured concrete. The grass just gave up where your feet kept landing, and now everyone walks that way without thinking. In MN 19, the Buddha says the mind works like that lawn, and he learned it by watching his own mind before his awakening. Today: what you think about often.
screen: `THE SAME WAY ACROSS THE LAWN.` → `A PATH NOBODY PLANNED.`

segments.voice: MN 19, the Dvedhavitakka, the discourse on two kinds of thought. Before his awakening, the Buddha says, he divided his thoughts into two piles. On one side: thoughts of sense desire, ill will and cruelty. On the other: thoughts of renunciation, goodwill and non-cruelty. When one from the first pile arose, he noticed it plainly: this leads to my own harm, to others' harm, to both; it obstructs wisdom. And as he noticed, it faded. Then comes the sentence. Whatever a monk keeps thinking about and pondering, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Think often of ill will, and the mind leans toward ill will. Think often of goodwill, and it leans toward goodwill. Then a picture from farm life. In the last month of the rainy season, when the crops are thick in the fields, a cowherd has to watch his cows constantly, tapping and checking them with a stick to keep them out of the crops, because he can see the trouble coming if they get in. But in the last month of the hot season, when the harvest is in, he can sit at the foot of a tree, or out in the open, and only needs to remember: there are the cows. At first, the work is watchful. Later, the mind leans the right way on its own, and you can rest. The Dhammapada opens on the same ground, in Max Müller's translation: “All that we are is the result of what we have thought.” A path across the lawn is made one step at a time.
screen: `TWO PILES OF THOUGHTS.` · `THE MIND INCLINES THAT WAY.` · `THE COWHERD BEFORE AND AFTER HARVEST.` · `ALL THAT WE ARE.` · then, large: `THE MIND INCLINES.`

segments.voice: Choose one good thing to think about on purpose: a person you're grateful for, a kindness someone showed you, a place that calms you. Let it fill the sit. When the mind wanders, and it will, walk it back to that one good thing, without scolding. You're making a path across the lawn: one more step on the same spot. The bell holds the time.
Vitakka, thought. Whatever the mind keeps returning to, it starts to lean toward.
Your line: the mind inclines. Today, come back to your one good thing at least five times: in a line, at a red light, before you open your phone. Day four hundred fourteen.

pairs: the cowherd watches with a stick

he sorted his thoughts into two piles.
the sutta says thoughts pass without shaping the mind
whatever one thinks about often becomes the mind's inclination.
after the harvest, the cowherd still has to watch every step
he can sit under a tree and simply remember: there are the cows.

fork.setup: the crops are harvested and the fields are bare. what does the cowherd in MN 19 need to do?
options: watch the cows every second
sit under a tree and just remember: there are the cows
sell the cows
fork.reveal: with no crops at risk, mindfulness is enough. the Buddha uses it for a mind that already leans toward the good.

original.note: Pali vitakka: thought, thinking; MN 19 is the dvedhā-vitakka, thoughts split in two.

trapdoor: what you thought: positive thinking.
what it means: whatever you think about often, the mind starts leaning that way, for good or ill.
what a scholar hears: dvedhā-vitakka means thought divided in two; the cowherd image moves from watchful restraint to easy mindfulness as the mind's inclination changes.

415.title: The carpenter's peg
415.hook: as a carpenter knocks out a coarse peg with a fine one, replace an unhelpful thought (MN 20)
415.howItsDone: Teachers who use MN 20's first method match an antidote to the kind of thought that arises, for example loving-kindness for ill will, following the commentary's examples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vitakka, and your line, the mind inclines. Did you come back to your one good thing five times? Day four hundred fifteen.

Old timber-frame houses were held together with wooden pegs driven through the joints. When a peg rots or splits, a carpenter can't just yank it out; that would wreck the joint. So one way to do it is to set a slimmer, harder peg against the end of the old one and tap. The new peg pushes the old one out and takes its place, and the joint is never left empty. Today: the carpenter's peg.
screen: `A ROTTEN PEG IN THE JOINT.` → `A FINER PEG, TAPPED IN.` → `NEVER LEFT EMPTY.`

segments.voice: We met this picture once before, on day three hundred eighty-five, as the first of five ways with a bad thought. Today, a closer look at the peg itself. MN 20, the Vitakkasanthana. When unwholesome thoughts, tied to desire, hate or delusion, keep arising while a person attends to some theme, the Buddha says, they should attend instead to another theme, one connected with what is wholesome. Then those thoughts fade, and the mind settles inwardly, grows still, becomes unified. Just as a skilled carpenter, or his apprentice, might knock out a coarse peg by means of a fine one. Read the picture slowly and three things stand out. First: the sutta doesn't say yank the thought out. It says attend to another theme, so the place isn't left empty. Second: the new peg has to fit the same hole. The later commentary gives examples: for desire fixed on a person, reflect on the body's unattractive parts; for ill will toward someone, loving-kindness; for confusion, ask someone wise, or examine causes with care. The replacement answers the same need. Third: it's a fine peg, finer than the old one. Not a bigger, louder thought. A quieter, truer one. The Dhammapada puts the craft in a line, in Max Müller's translation: “fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.” This is fashioning, one small joint at a time.
screen: `ATTEND TO ANOTHER THEME.` · `DON'T LEAVE THE HOLE EMPTY.` · `THE PEG MUST FIT THE HOLE.` · `FINER, NOT LOUDER.` · then, large: `A FINER PEG.`

segments.voice: Sit, and wait for a thought you'd rather not keep: a grudge, a craving, a worry. When it comes, ask what hole it's filling. Is it about a person, a want, a fear? Then choose a finer peg that fits the same hole. For the grudge, wish that person one simple good thing. For the craving, feel the body breathing. For the worry, name one honest next step. Tap it in gently. The bell holds the time.
Vitakka-santhana, the stilling of thoughts. A coarse thought knocked out by a finer one that fits the same place.
Your line: a finer peg. Today, when an old thought comes back, don't just pull at it; slide a finer one into its place. Day four hundred fifteen.

the commentary matches each replacement to the kind of thought
loving-kindness for ill will, for example.
the new peg should be a bigger, coarser one

fork.reveal: for ill will, loving-kindness: the replacement answers the same need, so it actually fits the hole.

original.note: Pali vitakka-saṇṭhāna: the stilling or settling of thoughts, the name of MN 20.

trapdoor: what you thought: swap a bad thought for a happy one.
what it means: answer an unhelpful thought with a finer one that fits the same need.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 20, Vitakkasanthana Sutta (the first method)

416.title: The last resort
416.hook: if nothing else works, clench the teeth, tongue to palate, and hold the mind down (MN 20)
416.howItsDone: Teachers who use MN 20 present its five methods in the sutta's order, from the gentlest to the most forceful, keeping the last for when the others have failed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vitakka-santhana, and your line, a finer peg. When an old thought came back, did a finer one fit into its place? Day four hundred sixteen.

Every good toolbox has a crowbar at the bottom. You don't start with it. You try the screwdriver, the wrench, the gentle tap with a hammer, a little oil on the hinge. But some days, something is really stuck, and you're glad the crowbar is there. MN 20 has a crowbar too. It's the fifth of five ways with an unwanted thought, and the Buddha puts it last on purpose. Today: the last resort.
screen: `A CROWBAR AT THE BOTTOM.` → `NOT THE FIRST TOOL.` → `BUT IT'S THERE.`

segments.voice: Day three hundred eighty-five walked through all five; here they are again, quickly, to show where the fifth sits. First, the finer peg: another theme, connected with the wholesome. If that fails, second: look at the danger in the thought, the way a young person who loves fine clothes would recoil if someone hung the carcass of a snake around their neck. If that fails, third: stop giving the thought attention, the way you'd shut your eyes or look away from something you don't want to see. Fourth: calm the thought down, step by step, like someone walking fast who asks, why am I hurrying? and slows down, then stands, then sits, then lies down. And only if all four fail, the fifth: with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of the mouth, beat down, constrain and crush mind with mind, the way a strong man might hold down a weaker one by the head or shoulders. It's startling language, and the text doesn't soften it: some days nothing gentle works. But notice where it sits: last. And notice something from MN 36. Describing his years of harsh practice before his awakening, the Buddha says he tried exactly this, teeth clenched, mind crushing mind, until sweat poured from his armpits. It didn't bring awakening. So force has a place on the path, but a small one, at the bottom of the box. The discourse ends with a promise: someone who has these five is a master of the courses of thought, thinking what they wish to think, and not what they don't.
screen: `FIVE TOOLS, IN ORDER.` · `DANGER, LOOKING AWAY, SLOWING DOWN.` · `TEETH CLENCHED: THE LAST RESORT.` · `MASTER OF THE COURSES OF THOUGHT.` · then, large: `THE LAST RESORT.`

segments.voice: No clenching today. Just the spirit of the fifth tool: staying. Bring to mind one hard moment, a recent one, small enough to hold. Let it come. If the body tightens, notice it, and breathe through it: in, and a long, slow out. Don't fix it, don't argue with it, don't run. Just hold steady, breath after breath, until it eases even a little. The bell holds the time.
Crowbar. When gentler ways fail, hold steady and hold the mind down: the fifth tool, kept for last.
Your line: a tool kept for last. Today, if something grips you, try the gentle tools first; if they fail, just hold on and breathe until it passes. Day four hundred sixteen.

screen: `DAY 416 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SIMILE OF THE SAW.`

417.title: The simile of the saw
417.hook: even if bandits sawed you limb from limb, keep a mind of goodwill (MN 21)
417.howItsDone: Teachers cite the simile of the saw when they teach patience, and some pair it with loving-kindness meditation directed toward difficult people.

segments.voice: Yesterday: crowbar, and your line, a tool kept for last. When something gripped you, did the gentle tools come first, and did you breathe until it passed? Day four hundred seventeen.

A monk named Moliya Phagguna spent a great deal of time with the nuns. When anyone criticized the nuns in front of him, he got angry and argued. When anyone criticized him in front of them, they got angry and argued. Word of it reached the Buddha. And what he said, first to Phagguna and then to all the monks, builds to a sentence that is hard to hear. Today: the simile of the saw.
screen: `PHAGGUNA, QUICK TO DEFEND.` → `CRITICISM, THEN ANGER.` → `A HARD SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: MN 21, the Kakacupama. The Buddha tells Phagguna: whatever anyone says, about the nuns or about you, train like this. My mind will not be changed. I won't utter harsh words. I'll stay compassionate, with a mind of goodwill, without inner hate. Then he lays out five ways people may speak to you: at the right time or the wrong time, truly or falsely, gently or harshly, helpfully or not, with goodwill or with hate. Any of the five may come. Your training stays the same. Then pictures, one after another. A man comes with a hoe and a basket to make the great earth not-earth. He digs, he scatters, he spits. He can't do it; the earth is too vast. So, the Buddha says, abide with a mind like the earth: vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility. Someone tries to paint pictures on empty space; there's nothing for the paint to cling to. Someone tries to boil the river Ganges with a blazing grass torch. Someone rubs a soft, well-cured catskin bag and tries to make it crackle. None of it works. And last, the hard sentence. Even if bandits were to cut you apart, limb by limb, with a two-handled saw, whoever let their mind turn to hate because of it would not be carrying out the teaching. It's the extreme case, set at the end as the floor. The Dhammapada says it in an old line, in Max Müller's translation: “hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love.”
screen: `FIVE WAYS PEOPLE MAY SPEAK.` · `A MIND LIKE THE EARTH.` · `PAINT ON SPACE, BURN THE GANGES.` · `EVEN WITH A SAW: NO HATE.` · then, large: `A MIND LIKE THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who criticizes you, lightly or often, fairly or not. Not the worst one; someone manageable. Notice what the body does when you picture them. Then picture the earth under you: wide, unbothered, taking footsteps and rain alike. Breathe out slowly, and see if you can wish that critic one ordinary good thing: a good night's sleep, maybe. If you can't today, that's honest. The earth can wait. The bell holds the time.
Kakacupama, the simile of the saw. Even under the cruelest treatment, keep a mind of goodwill, vast and steady as the earth.
Your line: a mind like the earth. Today, when a sharp word comes your way, let it fall on wide ground, and answer it later, if at all. Day four hundred seventeen.

fork.reveal: the torch can't touch it. a mind made vast with goodwill is like that: the harsh word has nothing to burn.

original.note: Pali kakacūpama: the simile of the saw; kakaca is a saw.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice even to bandits.
what it means: a mind so wide and steady, like the earth, that cruelty can't turn it to hate.
what a scholar hears: kakaca is a saw, and the Pali specifies a two-handled one; the same sutta also tells the story of the housewife Vedehikā and her maid.

418.title: Lady Vedehika
418.hook: a mistress famous for her calm is tested by her maid and loses her temper (MN 21)
418.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of Vedehika to show that patience is known only under provocation, and many practitioners treat everyday irritations as a chance to check their own calm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kakacupama, and your line, a mind like the earth. When a sharp word came, did it fall on wide ground? Day four hundred eighteen.

On day three hundred sixty-three, Vedehika got a few lines: the gentle lady of Savatthi, the maid who slept in, the blow. That telling stopped at the blow. The Buddha doesn't. In MN 21 he tells the story slowly, gives the maid a mind of her own, and then turns it on his listeners with a question the short version skipped: when someone stays calm, what is the calm resting on? Today: Lady Vedehika.
screen: `A STORY HEARD IN A FEW LINES.` → `THE MAID HAS A PLAN.` → `WHAT IS THE CALM RESTING ON?`

segments.voice: Start with Kali, because the text does. She isn't lazy. MN 21 calls her clever, diligent and neat in her work. That's what makes her test clean: there's no real fault to be angry at. Is my mistress truly calm, she wonders, or does the anger just never get a reason? So one morning she gets up late. Why so late, Kali? No reason, madam. No reason, you wicked girl, and you get up so late? A frown. The next morning, later. Sharper words. The third morning, later still, and Vedehika grabs the pin of the door bolt and strikes her on the head, and it bleeds. Kali goes out and tells the neighbors, and the famous reputation turns. Then the Buddha's first point. A monk can seem very gentle, very meek, very peaceful, as long as disagreeable words don't touch him. Then his second point, the one the short telling left out. He won't call a monk easy to correct if he's easy to correct only so the robes and food keep coming, because when they stop, so does the gentleness. Only someone who is gentle out of respect for the teaching itself, he says, is truly easy to correct. So the story holds two tests. Vedehika's calm was resting on nobody pushing. Some calm rests on getting something for it. The Buddha is asking which kind his own monks have. The story is told to them, not about her, so its edge points inward, at whoever is listening.
screen: `KALI, CLEVER AND DILIGENT.` · `THE THIRD DAY: THE DOOR PIN.` · `GENTLE ONLY FOR ROBES AND FOOD?` · `THE EDGE POINTS INWARD.` · then, large: `CALM, TESTED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind something mildly irritating: a slow line, a late reply, a noise from next door. Picture it happening once. Then a second time. Then a third. Watch closely: where does your calm start to thin? The jaw, the breath, words beginning to form? You're not failing. You're doing what Kali did, but kindly: finding out. Then let the picture go and rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Lady Vedehika. Famous for her calm, until her maid tested it: gentleness is known only when it's tried.
Your line: calm, tested. Today, when something small goes wrong a second time, notice your calm before you notice the problem. Day four hundred eighteen.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (the story of Vedehika and Kali)

419.title: The water snake
419.hook: grasping the teaching wrongly is like grabbing a snake by the tail (MN 22)
419.howItsDone: Teachers cite the water snake simile as a warning against studying the teaching for debate or status, and encourage students to apply what they learn to themselves first.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lady Vedehika, and your line, calm, tested. When something small went wrong a second time, did you notice your calm first? Day four hundred nineteen.

A forked stick is about the simplest tool there is: a branch with a V at one end. In MN 22 it's the difference between being bitten and walking away safe. Grab a snake by the tail, and it whips around and bites the hand that's holding it. Pin it first, then take it behind the head, and it can't. The Buddha used that picture for something unexpected: how people hold on to his own teaching. Today: the water snake.
screen: `A FORKED STICK.` → `NEVER BY THE TAIL.` → `PIN IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: MN 22, the Alagaddupama, the simile of the water snake. It begins with a monk named Arittha, who had come to a wrong view: that the things the Buddha called obstacles weren't really obstacles to someone who indulged in them. The other monks tried to talk him out of it. He held on. So the Buddha called him in, and was blunt: misguided man, when have you ever heard me teach it that way? Then he turned to everyone. Some people, he said, learn the teaching, the discourses, the verses, the stories, but don't examine its meaning with wisdom. They learn it so they can criticize others and win arguments. And so the teaching harms them, the way a man looking for a water snake might find a big one and grab it by the coils or by the tail. It turns and bites his hand or his arm, and he suffers, even to death. Why? Because he grasped it wrongly. Others learn the teaching, examine its meaning, and don't use it to win arguments, and it leads to their welfare for a long time. Like a man who pins the snake down with a forked stick, then takes it firmly by the neck. It can coil all over his arm, and it won't bite. The striking thing is where the danger sits. Not in the teaching. In the grip. The Dhammapada has a line for someone who knows the words without living them, in Max Müller's translation: “like a cowherd counting the cows of others.”
screen: `ARITTHA HOLDS A WRONG VIEW.` · `LEARNED TO WIN ARGUMENTS.` · `GRABBED BY THE TAIL, IT BITES.` · `PINNED, THEN HELD BY THE NECK.` · then, large: `HOLD IT RIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Pick one teaching that matters to you, from this path or anywhere in your life. Hold it in mind. Then check your grip. Do you use it mostly to look at yourself, or mostly to measure other people? Do you understand it, or mostly quote it? No verdict needed. Just notice where your hand is: on the tail, or behind the head. Then let it rest, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
alagadda. A teaching grasped wrongly bites; held rightly, for understanding and not for winning, it helps.
Your line: hold it rightly. Today, if you catch yourself using something you believe to win an argument, put it down and ask what it says to you. Day four hundred nineteen.

pairs: held on to a wrong view

the danger is in the grip: learning it to criticize and win arguments.
MN 22 warns against learning the teaching to win arguments
that's the wrong grip that gets you bitten.
the Buddha gently agreed with Arittha
he called him a misguided man and corrected the view.

options: grab it by the tail, fast

leave it alone forever
fork.reveal: pin first, then hold behind the head. it can coil all over his arm and it won't bite. that's the right grip on a teaching.

original.note: Pali alagadda: a water snake, the snake of MN 22's simile.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning against dangerous ideas.
what it means: the danger is in the grip: a teaching held to win arguments bites the one holding it.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (Arittha and the water snake)

420.title: The raft
420.hook: the raft is for crossing, not for carrying on your head afterward (MN 22)
420.howItsDone: The raft simile is taught in Theravada, Zen and Tibetan settings as a reminder that practices and doctrines are means, not ends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: alagadda, and your line, hold it rightly. Did you catch yourself using something you believe to win, and put it down? Day four hundred twenty, the end of the week.

A man on a long journey comes to a wide stretch of water. On this side: danger. On the far side: safety. No ferry. No bridge. So he gathers grass, sticks, branches and leaves, ties them into a raft, and paddles across with his hands and feet. He makes it. And standing on the far bank, with the dripping raft at his feet, he has a thought: this raft was so useful to me. Shouldn't I take it with me? Today: the raft.
screen: `A RIVER, NO FERRY.` → `A RAFT OF GRASS AND STICKS.` → `SHOULDN'T I TAKE IT WITH ME?`

segments.voice: This is also MN 22, the same discourse as yesterday's water snake. The Buddha asks the monks: if the man lifted the raft onto his head and carried it wherever he went, would he be doing what should be done with a raft? No, they say. Then the Buddha gives the answer himself: haul it up onto dry land, or leave it floating in the water, and go on your way. Then the Buddha says: I have taught you the teaching as a raft, for crossing over, not for holding on to. And he adds a line that readers take in more than one way: understanding the simile of the raft, you should let go even of good things, how much more so of bad things. The Pali word is dhamma, which can mean the teaching, or good states and qualities. Some read the line as: even the teaching is let go once it has done its work. The old commentary reads it as: let go even of attachment to calm and insight. Both say: don't cling. Neither says: throw the raft away before you've crossed. That part is easy to miss. The man is on the far bank when he sets it down; in the middle of the river, you hold on and paddle. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: “Few are there among men who arrive at the other shore.” And the week looks back: what you think about often, the finer peg, the last resort, the saw, Lady Vedehika, alagadda, and the raft. Seven pictures, each one meant to be used.
screen: `CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD?` · `FOR CROSSING, NOT FOR HOLDING.` · `LET GO EVEN OF GOOD THINGS.` · `ONLY ONCE YOU'VE CROSSED.` · then, large: `PUT THE RAFT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one thing that once helped you across something: a habit, a routine, an app, a belief about yourself, a way of coping that worked back then. Ask honestly: am I still crossing, or am I on the bank, carrying it? If you're still crossing, keep paddling; that's fine. If you're across, picture setting it down on dry ground, with thanks. The bell holds the time.
The raft. The teaching is for crossing over, not for carrying on your head once you're across.
Your line: put the raft down. Today, let go of one thing you're done with: a habit, an old grudge, a file, a rule you don't need anymore. Day four hundred twenty.

the man sets it down on the far bank, not mid-river.
the raft is in the same discourse as the water snake
both are in MN 22.
the monks say he should carry the raft on his head
they say no; then the Buddha says to leave it on land or in the water and go on.

fork.setup: you've crossed the river on your homemade raft. what does the Buddha say to do with it?
options: carry it on your head; it was so useful
leave it on the bank or in the water, and go on
burn it so nobody else can use it
fork.reveal: leave it and go on. the teaching is for crossing, not for holding on to, and you only set it down once you're across.

original.note: Pali kulla: a raft; the simile is called kullūpama, the raft simile.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says throw away the teachings.
what it means: the teaching is a raft, used fully for crossing and set down only on the far shore.
what a scholar hears: in 'dhammā pi vo pahātabbā', dhamma may mean teachings or good states; the commentary reads it as attachment to calm and insight.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft)
